Ashtavakra Gita: awareness within experience

The Ashtavakra Gita (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā), also called the Ashtavakra Samhita, presents a dialogue between Ashtavakra and Janaka on non-dual Self-knowledge. The following summaries are paraphrases, with chapter and verse references; they are not quotations.

Understand the Creator and the gameBring remembrance into daily lifeRecognize the same Creator in others

We are the Creator. We created this game of experiences and entered it. Having designed it before entering, we cannot change its design from inside the game.

How Uday’s game story makes this understanding concrete

Awareness beyond the role · 1.3, 1.6, 1.12

These verses distinguish the witnessing Self from the elements, mental pleasure and pain, and individual doership. The Self is described as free, peaceful awareness. This connects with Uday’s distinction between the shared Creator and the role absorbed in a scene. Remembering the Creator who designed and entered the game can invite enquiry into whether a passing thought describes our whole identity.

  • Sanskrit text · chapter 1
  • John Richards translation · chapter 1 (PDF)

One Self, many lives · 2.4, 15.6

Verse 2.4 compares the world and Self to waves and water. Verse 15.6 asks the reader to recognize the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, relinquishing ego and possessiveness. Uday applies shared identity to relationships: the person who disagrees is another expression of the same Creator within the game. Addressing a disagreement can unfold with that remembrance.

  • Sanskrit text · chapters 2 and 15
  • John Richards translation · chapters 2 and 15 (PDF)

The source and the unfolding · 11.2–4

These verses connect peace with recognition of Ishvara as the maker of all, acceptance of adversity and prosperity arising through fate in time, and action without inner attachment. They provide a close connection with surrender in Uday’s philosophy. His further account says that we designed the game before entering and cannot rewrite its design from inside. Planning, helping, and deciding remain parts of that unfolding; these verses do not independently establish the complete account.

  • Sanskrit text · chapter 11
  • John Richards translation · chapter 11 (PDF)

Experience without being inwardly bound · 7.2

Janaka compares himself to an ocean unaffected in its fullness by the rising and falling of the world’s waves. Uday’s movie and lotus images offer a related way to explore participation with inward lightness. Their practical invitation is to remember the Creator during the scene, while allowing experience to unfold within the design. The ocean belongs to this text; the movie and lotus explanations here are Uday’s.

  • Sanskrit text · chapter 7
  • John Richards translation · chapter 7 (PDF)

Compassion and honesty at the beginning · 1.2

Ashtavakra’s opening guidance includes forgiveness, sincerity, compassion, contentment, and truthfulness. This helps readers connect Self-enquiry with everyday conduct. In Uday’s framework, care develops through recognizing the same Creator in other lives. Repairing harm or seeking help is participation within the game.

  • Sanskrit text · verse 1.2
  • John Richards translation · chapter 1 (PDF)

Ashtavakra emphasizes the Self as already free and beyond individual doership. Uday brings a related insight into the Creator-and-game story, making identity and remembrance easier to visualize. Read their connection through the verses above: the game designed before entry is Uday’s explanation, while the cited passages develop awareness, oneness, and surrender.

Try this now

Recall a scene that absorbed you: criticism, waiting, or a changed plan. In Uday’s teaching, remember the shared Creator who designed and entered the game, whose design cannot be rewritten from inside. What is the role feeling? What notices it? How might remembrance include the other person and the response available now? Observe honestly, including if nothing changes.
